sentences.text: The holotype specimen, which is the specific fossil used to define the species, consists of a partial skeleton including a skull from the Aptian-aged Twin Mountains Formation.
This individual was a subadult, estimated to be between 2.5 and 3 meters long, meaning the full adult size of the animal remains unknown.
A unique feature of this dinosaur is that its premaxilla, the bone at the very front of the upper jaw, bears four teeth with a vertical trough on the outside.
The neck vertebrae are opisthocoelous, a condition where the bones are convex at the front and concave at the rear.
The name Convolosaurus means "flocking lizard" because fossils were found in a dense concentration at Proctor Lake in Texas.

Fossils from this site have been combined into three mounted skeletons displayed at the Proctor Lake US Army Corps of Engineers Office, the Perot Museum of Nature and Science, and the Fort Worth Museum of Science and History.
James "Rusty" Branch discovered the fossil site in May 1985, noting it was one of the richest Lower Cretaceous sites in North America.

The discovery of the site was reported in the scientific literature in 1988, but the species Convolosaurus marri was formally named and described in 2019 by Kate A. Andrzejewski, Dale A. Winkler, and Louis Leo Jacobs.
The genus Convolosaurus was described by Andrzejewski and colleagues in 2019.
Only one fossil occurrence of Convolosaurus has been recorded so far.
Convolosaurus is classified within the dinosaur class Ornithischia and belongs to the family Tenontosauridae.
Although initially thought to be a member of Hypsilophodontidae, Convolosaurus was classified in 2019 as a basal ornithopod above Hypsilophodon and below Thescelosaurus.
The placement of Convolosaurus reversed previous views because it shares two supraorbitals with Thescelosaurus, suggesting Hypsilophodon lost this trait independently.
Convolosaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Aptian age, which spans between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago.
This places the animal in North America approximately 125 million years ago during the middle Cretaceous.
